beliefs.practice: Read the cluster connection string from an environment variable (DOCUMENTDB_URI) at runtime; never embed credentials in code, config files committed to the repo, or printed to logs.
Enable TLS/SSL on the MongoDB driver connection and validate server certificates (e.g., tls=true/ssl=true and tlsAllowInvalidCertificates=false) to encrypt traffic to the DocumentDB cluster.

Use a pooled MongoClient with explicit maxPoolSize and socketTimeoutMS settings (configure connection pool sizing appropriate for expected concurrency, e.g., maxPoolSize=50) rather than opening/closing a new client per request.
Seed data idempotently using upsert or bulkWrite with ordered=false so repeated runs do not create duplicates and are efficient (use a unique sales_id key and bulk operations for large loads).

Choose a high-cardinality, immutable partition key for the collection to avoid hot partitions (for example a store_id or region_id rather than a low-cardinality season field) and design documents so the chosen key is present and stable.

Create indexes that support the aggregation pipeline: add an index on {category:1, date:1} (or {season:1, category:1, date:1} if season is queried frequently) so $match/$sort stages are covered and the pipeline can be executed efficiently.

When queries compute seasonal sales velocity, push $match and $project to the start of the aggregation pipeline (filter by date range and category first, then project only needed fields) to minimize processed data.
Use server-side aggregation pipelines (MongoDB aggregate) rather than pulling raw documents into the app and computing metrics client-side to reduce network transfer and leverage DB compute.

Handle transient network and server errors with retries using exponential backoff, and distinguish idempotent vs non-idempotent operations (retry only idempotent reads/aggregation; for writes use upsert or ensure idempotency tokens).

For the vector-capable cluster, ensure vector fields have an index created with appropriate algorithm and parameters (e.g., HNSW or IVF options such as M/efConstruction or nlist) and that the index dimension and metric match the stored vectors before running k-NN queries.
Keep vector dimensionality consistent across all documents, and store vectors in a typed array or fixed-length list field; validate vector length at insert time to avoid index/query failures.

When performing approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) queries, tune query-time parameters (e.g., ef/runtime search size) to balance recall vs latency and record those settings as part of the tool configuration.
Before adding or changing indexes, run explain() or use the MCP server tools to verify the aggregation/query plan uses the intended index and to measure I/O and RU/ops cost.

Provision sufficient throughput (RU/s or appropriate cluster tier) for expected aggregation workloads and enable autoscale where available to handle spikes from periodic batch aggregation or agent runs.

Limit database credentials to least privilege required (create a database user with only read on the sales collection for the agent's analysis tool; separate a different key/user for administrative seeding tasks).

Use timeouts on external web-search requests and a deterministic fallback (mock) so the LangChain agent remains responsive if the search API is slow or unavailable; apply retries/timeouts and circuit breaker patterns.
When seeding large datasets, use bulkWrite in batches (e.g., 1k–10k docs per batch) and monitor for rate limiting or RU exhaustion; slow down or back off if you see throughput throttling errors.
Minimize the fields returned by queries (use projection) and paginate with range-based cursors where possible to avoid large in-memory result sets and to reduce RU/latency.

Store temporal fields in UTC using BSON Date objects and design seasonal comparisons with explicit date ranges (avoid storing local-time strings) so aggregations on date arithmetic are correct and index-friendly.
Log operations, query parameters, pipeline shapes, and costs (RU/latency) but scrub or redact any secrets; keep sufficient telemetry to diagnose slow aggregations or index misses.
